note: Published 7 Aug from an in-session research run (the headless CLI has been logged out since 4 Aug). Covers through the 6 Aug US close. The 7 Aug Asia session is NOT included — this run gathered data on 6 Aug and the 7 Aug sessions had not closed when it was verified. 23 items gathered, every one re-opened and confirmed against its source; none dropped. Includes a correction to our own prior file — see the index-level item.

items.headline: 6 Aug reversal — Dow sheds 464 points as Brent rebounds nearly 4% and yields move higher
items.summary: Stocks fell on 6 Aug. The Dow closed at 53,885.10, down 464.02 points or 0.85%; the S&P 500 fell 13.59 points, or 0.18%, to 7,709.96; the Nasdaq composite eased 15.09 points, or 0.06%, to 26,348.35; the Russell 2000 fell 0.6% to 3,001.55. The driver was a reversal in the Iran/Hormuz de-escalation trade: Brent crude climbed nearly 4% on renewed concern over Iran and continued worries about shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and US Treasury yields moved higher ahead of the employment report. Sector rotation continued, with energy outperforming while technology traded unevenly. Single-name moves included Warner Bros. Discovery up on stronger-than-expected results, Honeywell Aerospace down on weaker earnings, Western Digital and SanDisk sharply lower after disappointing earnings, AppLovin and Datadog down on guidance misses, and SpaceX higher after a lockup expiration.
items.actionable: This is the single most important development versus the 4 Aug dashboard state: the Hormuz de-escalation that drove the record run is NOT settled, and oil round-tripped a meaningful part of the crash within two sessions. Do not carry "oil crashed, risk-off is over" as the standing narrative. For his book the combination is awkward — higher oil supports the energy sleeve but the accompanying move to a 4.67% 10Y and 5.21% 30Y raises the discount rate on SG REITs (Keppel REIT, Mapletree), the developers (CityDev, UOL, Wing Tai) and the levered silver carry simultaneously.

items.headline: Challenger job cuts fall to a two-year low in July — 33,429 cuts, AI the top reason for a fifth straight month
items.summary: Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on 6 August that US employers announced 33,429 job cuts in July — the lowest monthly total in two years, and the lowest since July 2024's 25,885 — down 27% from June's 45,849 and down 46% from July 2025's 62,075. Artificial intelligence was the leading stated reason for the fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts, 33% of the July total. Announced hiring plans rose 47% to 16,095 from June's 10,933, versus just 3,200 in July 2025. Year-to-date announced cuts total 477,033, down 41% from 806,383 in the first seven months of 2025. Separately — and NOT from the Challenger report — the Department of Labor's weekly release the same morning showed initial jobless claims for the week ending 1 August rose 1,000 to 199,000, with the prior week revised up from 197,000 to 198,000, holding below the 200,000 mark; the four-week moving average fell 4,500 to 198,750 from 203,250, while continuing claims for the week ending 25 July rose 24,000 to 1,801,000. Note the internal tension in that pair: initial claims say almost nobody is being fired, but the rise in continuing claims says those who do lose jobs are taking longer to be rehired.
items.actionable: Counts against the dovish read of the ADP miss. Soft survey-based hiring but firm hard data — claims under 200K and layoffs at a two-year low — means the Fed has no labour-market cover to stop tightening if inflation stays hot. Read as hike-supportive, therefore adverse for the ~1.6x levered silver leg, which is the largest single risk in the book and the most sensitive to both real yields and IBKR margin cost.

items.headline: Silver opens at $62.20, its highest open since June — but flat vs Wednesday's close; the 4% jump belongs to the 5 Aug session
items.summary: Silver September futures opened at $62.20/oz on Thursday 6 Aug, down 0.1% from Wednesday's close but up over 4% from Wednesday's OPENING price — i.e. the big leg happened during the 5 Aug session, not on 6 Aug. By 9:12 a.m. ET on 6 Aug it had eased to $61.73. Yahoo Finance notes the last time silver opened above $62 with any real consistency was in June, and puts silver +64.7% year-on-year. Corroborating spot prints on 6 Aug from other outlets: Fortune quotes spot at $61.83/oz at 7:00 a.m. ET, +0.60% (+$0.37) vs the prior day's 7 a.m. print of $61.46, and +63.48% vs $37.82 a year ago; Golden State Mint's daily report quotes $61.30/oz and notes silver has climbed more than 4% from Monday's open. Note the honest discrepancy: these figures come from different snapshot conventions at different vendors, so treat ~$61.3–$62.2 as the 6 Aug trading band rather than a single number. Stated drivers: Hormuz reopening negotiations plus the ADP payrolls miss, both of which cut the odds of a September Fed HIKE. Two cautions on the technical read. Silver is down 0.7% versus one month ago, so this is a recovery to the top of a range, not a breakout to new highs. And both sources treat the $60 level as an open question rather than established support — Yahoo writes that "it's unclear how long silver can hold at the $60-plus price point," while Golden State Mint flags whether it can hold above $60 as the thing to watch, noting it spent much of July trying to do so.
items.actionable: This is the position that matters at ~1.6x. Silver did NOT follow oil down — it rallied into the oil crash, which confirms the current driver is the Fed/labour-market channel, not the geopolitical risk premium. The margin-relevant observation: the whole 4% move is leaning on one soft data point (ADP), and the July non-farm payrolls print lands Friday 7 Aug at 8:30 a.m. ET. A levered position sized against a $60 support level has that level tested by a single number roughly 24 hours from now. Worth knowing where your maintenance margin sits before the print rather than after.

items.headline: Gold jumps 2.38% to $4,270.62 and opens at $4,307, its first open above $4,300 since 17 June
items.summary: Fortune, in a dated 6 Aug article, quotes gold spot at $4,270.62/oz at 7:00 a.m. ET, up $99.63 (+2.38%) from the previous day's 7 a.m. print of $4,170.99. The same piece puts gold +2.27% versus one month ago ($4,175.69) and +26.75% year-on-year (versus $3,369.27) — all figures confirmed verbatim against the source. Yahoo Finance's 6 Aug report separately has gold OPENING at $4,307/troy oz, its first open above $4,300 since 17 June, and attributes the move to progress toward a partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz together with ADP's soft July jobs print. Confirmed vendor prints on 6 Aug therefore span roughly $4,270 to $4,307 depending on snapshot time.
items.actionable: Direct answer to the question you asked: YES, the metals held their bid through both the oil crash and the yield backup, and did considerably better than hold — gold added ~2.4% in a single session while WTI fell and the 10Y rose. That is a meaningful regime signal. Through June-July gold traded as a war hedge and moved WITH oil; on 5-6 Aug it inverted and traded as a rate-expectations asset, rallying because cheaper oil plus weak jobs equals a lower chance of a September hike. For the miners sleeve (GDX, SILJ, SLVP), gold back above $4,250 with silver above $60 is a strong joint margin environment.

items.headline: WTI down 11% over three sessions to ~$75 as Iran and Oman agree a Hormuz shipping route — but it is a 2-4 month corridor, not a reopening
items.summary: The Irish Times, published 6 Aug 2026, reports that WTI lost 11 per cent over the first three sessions of the week, with Brent trading near $79/bbl and WTI around $75/bbl. It states the proposed Strait of Hormuz shipping route 'would remain active for two to four months, although the agreement does not mean a full reopening, according to Iranian officials.' Reuters (carried by The Star, same date) quotes a small bounce at 0640 GMT: Brent +46 cents to $79.91/bbl (+0.58%) and WTI +36 cents to $75.58/bbl (+0.48%). On substance, Reuters has Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei saying Wednesday that Iran and Oman reached an understanding on the geographic coordinates for a shipping route, with a joint announcement being finalised 'provided certain third parties did not interfere' — described as one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran, against which US officials 'have repeatedly insisted they would never agree to Iran controlling access to one of the world's most important trade routes for energy supplies.' Offsetting bullish news the same day: Yemen's Houthis said they struck a Saudi oil tanker off the Red Sea port of Yanbu and another in the Gulf of Aden, neither confirmed by Saudi Arabia. Gulf crude and condensate exports were largely steady in July and remain about 40% below pre-war levels.
items.actionable: Against your 4 Aug baseline of WTI ~$79-82, crude has taken another leg down to ~$75, so the de-escalation trade has extended rather than exhausted. But read the fine print before treating the Hormuz risk premium as gone: a 2-4 month corridor that Iran explicitly says is not a reopening, that hands Tehran control of transit, and that the US has rejected, is a fragile construct — one analyst quoted by Reuters notes traders still remember the June MOU that collapsed. Exports still 40% below pre-war. The energy sleeve is the direct casualty; the read-through to the rest of the book is that cheaper crude is exactly what is suppressing hike odds and supporting your metals.

items.headline: 10Y yield backs up more than 5bp to 4.67% on 6 Aug — gold rallied through it anyway
items.summary: TradingEconomics' US 10-year Treasury series records the yield rising to 4.67% on 6 Aug 2026, up 0.06 percentage points (more than 5 basis points) from the previous session. The same page reports markets pricing roughly a 58% chance of a 25bp Fed hike in September. Transparency note: this source is a live quote board that had already rolled forward to 7 Aug when read, so it is a dated data series rather than a fixed-date document; the 6 Aug level and move are taken from the series' own 6 Aug data point and its description of the immediately preceding session. A previously stated 18-month high of 4.75% earlier in the week could not be confirmed and has been removed, as has an unverified third-party preview of Friday's July non-farm payrolls.
items.actionable: The second half of your question — did metals hold through the yield backup — is answered here, and the answer is a clean yes. Gold added 2.38% on 6 Aug on a day the 10Y rose more than 5bp. Real-yield-driven gold selling did not happen; the Fed-path story dominated. The forward risk is symmetric and dated: a September hike is only ~58-59% priced, and the range of payroll estimates for Friday is enormous (+10K to +140K, versus consensus ~+80K). A print at the top of that range pushes hike odds up, yields up, and pressures a levered silver position on the same day; a print near the bottom does the reverse. This is the near-term event risk concentrated on one release.

items.headline: Bitcoin firm but rangebound at ~$64.2k; ETH outperforms at +2.1%
items.summary: Yahoo Finance reports bitcoin opened at $64,602.32 on Thursday 6 Aug, up 0.9% versus Wednesday's opening price, and had eased to $64,216.91 by 9:40 a.m. ET. Ethereum opened at $1,906.96, up 2.1% versus Wednesday, and traded $1,901.84 at 9:40 a.m. ET. Both opened at their highest levels of the week and both show positive month-over-month gains. Stated drivers are identical to the metals: investors easing back into risk assets on the Hormuz negotiations, plus the underwhelming July ADP report, with both factors reducing the odds of a rate increase after the Fed's September meeting.
items.actionable: BTC is participating in the same 'no September hike' trade as gold and silver but with visibly less conviction — 0.9% against gold's 2.38% and silver's ~4% two-day move. Worth noting for cross-asset read: your precious metals are not simply riding a generic risk-on wave, they are outperforming the risk-on complex, which is consistent with a genuine monetary-policy bid rather than beta. ETH's 2.1% outpacing BTC is the only notable relative move in the crypto sleeve.

items.headline: DBS posts record S$3.08b Q2 profit and RAISES FY2026 guidance; STI climbs ~1.1% and DBS hits lifetime high while the rest of Asia sells off
items.summary: DBS reported 2Q/1H FY2026 on 6 Aug: net profit S$3,079m (+9% y/y from S$2,824m), total income S$6,093m (+6% y/y), surpassing the S$6 billion mark in a quarter for the first time. Net interest income S$3,581m. NIM compressed to 1.87% from 2.05% a year earlier. ROE rose to 17.9% from 16.7%. Dividend declared at 81 Singapore cents (66c ordinary + 15c capital return), up 6c y/y; ex-dividend 14 Aug 2026. Critically, management RAISED guidance: total income now expected to exceed 2025 levels, group NII expected to close the gap to 2025 levels, and commercial-book non-interest income growth lifted to the mid-teens led by wealth management; cost-income ratio guided to stay in the low-40% range. Reuters (via The Star) reported the STI advanced 1.1% on the day and DBS shares rose 3% to a lifetime high — a decoupling from the regional rout, with the MSCI EM Asia index down almost 2% the same session. I could not confirm the exact STI closing level or the exact DBS closing price at document level.
items.actionable: The guidance RAISE is the substantive item, not the headline beat — DBS is guiding NII to recover toward 2025 levels despite NIM falling 18bp y/y, with mid-teens non-II growth doing the work. Watch whether OCBC and UOB echo this in the remainder of SG bank earnings season; if they do, the SGD-asset side of his book is being repriced on fee/wealth income rather than rates. Note the 14 Aug ex-dividend date for the 81c payout. Also note DBS traded at roughly 3.0x price-to-book on the pre-results 5 Aug close of S$73.55 versus a ~1.5x historical average (per Growbeansprout) — the re-rating is already substantial. Not advice, just the arithmetic.

items.headline: Korea crashes: Kospi -4.58% to 6,296.38, sell-side sidecar triggered, SK Hynix -10.37% and Samsung -6.3% on AI-capex profitability fears
items.summary: The Kospi fell 301.88 points, or 4.58%, to close at 6,296.38 on 6 Aug, having touched an intraday low of 6,238.32. The Korea Exchange activated a sell-side sidecar for five minutes at 10:18 a.m., halting program trading in Kospi-listed shares. SK Hynix plunged 10.37% to about 1.5 million won; Samsung Electronics fell 6.3% to 203,500 won. Foreigners sold a net 3.33 trillion won of stock and institutions a further 121.8 billion won, while individuals bought a net 3.34 trillion won. Analysts attributed the move to losses in US chip stocks and profit-taking, with investors sceptical about the profitability of large-scale AI infrastructure spending despite recent strong tech earnings. Reuters (via The Star) recorded the Kospi down as much as 5.5% intraday, Samsung down as much as 6.7%, SK Hynix down as much as 9.8%, TSMC -1.9% and Taiwan stocks down as much as 1.3%. On the currency: the won touched 1,414.5 per USD intraday, its strongest since early October 2025, but did not hold it, closing at 1,423.8 — weaker by 0.7 won on the session. So there was no disorderly currency flight, but no net won strengthening either.
items.actionable: This is the read-through channel to his HK/China tech sleeve, specifically SMIC (0981). The trigger was scepticism about AI capex returns rather than any Asia-specific shock, so it is a global-tech-multiple event, not a China-policy event. The won strengthening while equities crashed is worth noting — it argues foreign selling was sector rotation rather than a broad Asia de-risking, which is a materially different signal for his SGD cash and SG bank exposure. Watch whether the sidecar-level panic follows through or mean-reverts in the next session.

items.headline: Hang Seng -1.5% to 25,530 in tech retreat, but Shanghai Composite BUCKS the rout and closes higher at 3,900
items.summary: Hong Kong fell on 6 Aug: the Hang Seng Index dropped 385 points, or 1.5%, to 25,530 on turnover of HK$255.23 billion. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 112 points, or 2.3%, to 4,820, and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index fell 105 points, or 1.2%, to 8,498. RTHK attributed the decline to renewed concerns about AI investment profitability following disappointing earnings from US tech firms SanDisk and Western Digital. Mainland markets diverged from Hong Kong: the Shanghai Composite ROSE 21 points, or 0.57%, to 3,900, while the Shenzhen Component fell 34 points, or 0.24%, to 14,110. IMPORTANT GAP: no document I loaded gave individual closing moves for Tencent (0700), Xiaomi (1810) or SMIC (0981) on this date. An investing.com article describing Tencent, Xiaomi, Alibaba and Baidu losing 2-4% was dated 17 July 2026, not 6 August, and is therefore excluded.
items.actionable: The A-share/H-share divergence is the signal: Shanghai up 0.57% while HSI fell 1.5% on the same day means the selling was foreign-flow and global-AI-multiple driven, not a domestic China demand or policy shock. That distinction matters for how he reads his 0700/1810/0981 sleeve. Do NOT put stock-level moves for Tencent, Xiaomi or SMIC on the dashboard for this date — I could not confirm them, and the Xiaomi position (26,662 units) is large enough that a guessed number would be exactly the kind of error that got retracted last week. Re-verify stock-level moves from an HKEX or exchange-sourced page before publishing any.

items.headline: Japan round trip: Nikkei +3.66% to 66,300.44 on 5 Aug on an AI-led rally and Hormuz de-escalation, then gives back 617 points to 65,683.26 on 6 Aug
items.summary: On 5 Aug the Nikkei 225 closed at 66,300.44, up 2,342.91 points or 3.66%, its best close since 23 July; the TOPIX rose 84.39 points, or 2.13%, to 4,046.17. Two independent documents confirm these figures. The lead driver was a surge in AI-related shares, with the semiconductor index rising for a fourth consecutive session after having fallen 20.6% in July; alongside that, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated a US-Iran agreement to resume safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz could be reached soon, falling US crude futures eased inflation concerns, and the prior session set a record Wall Street close (Dow +907.47 points to a record 54,085.88). Leaders were AI and semiconductor names: Advantest +8.77%, Murata +9.82%, Fanuc +4.41%, Tokyo Electron +3.26%, plus banks Mizuho +4.17% and MUFG +2.05%; decliners included Daikin -6.31% and Fast Retailing -2.33%. On 6 Aug the Nikkei reversed, closing at 65,683.26, down 617.18 points, after falling nearly 1,000 points intraday, on US tech weakness and profit-taking; selling concentrated in semiconductor names that had reported strong earnings, with participants noting stocks were being sold on the news. TSE Prime volume was 2.9973 billion shares on turnover of 9.688087 trillion yen. No percentage change for 6 Aug was stated in the source, so none is quoted here.
items.actionable: The 5 Aug leg is the important confirmation for his oil/energy sleeve: the Hormuz-reopening story he had as of 4 Aug was still intact and still driving risk appetite on 5 Aug, with Bessent named on the record. That de-escalation held into 6 Aug — the 6 Aug reversal was an AI-capex story, NOT a geopolitical re-escalation. Keep those two threads separate on the dashboard. Net over two sessions Japan is still up strongly from the 4 Aug base, unlike Korea and Hong Kong. Still pending as of 6 Aug: I found no confirmation that a Hormuz deal was actually signed — it remained prospective.

items.headline: DBS Q2 FY2026 net profit +9% to record S$3.08b; quarterly income crosses S$6b for the first time; 81-cent dividend and a raised FY2026 outlook
items.summary: DBS reported 2Q FY2026 net profit of S$3.08b, up 9% y/y, with total income crossing S$6b in a single quarter for the first time (S$6.09b, +6% y/y) — both records; 1H net profit was S$6.01b. Net interest margin narrowed 18bp to 1.87% in the quarter (1H: -20bp to 1.88%) on lower rates, offset by fee and wealth income; NPL ratio 1.0%. Declared total dividend of 81.0 cents per share (66.0c ordinary interim + 15.0c capital return). Per Reuters, management RAISED its FY2026 outlook: total income is now expected to exceed 2025 levels, versus earlier guidance of 'around' 2025 levels, and commercial-book non-interest income growth guidance was lifted to the mid-teens from high single digits, led by wealth management. The dividend timetable — ex-date 14 Aug 2026, record date 17 Aug 2026, payment 25 Aug 2026 — and the guidance raise are not stated in the dbs.com release itself and are sourced to the 6 Aug results coverage; the headline financials above are from dbs.com, dated 06 Aug 2026.
items.actionable: Ex-dividend is 14 Aug 2026 (record 17 Aug, paid 25 Aug) — a near-term calendar item for the DBS position. The guidance raise is the genuine new information versus the 4 Aug dashboard. The offsetting negative to monitor is NIM compression (-18bp to 1.87%) as rates fall: DBS is now visibly funding earnings growth from wealth/fee income rather than spread.

items.headline: MP Materials Q2 2026: NdPr sales +127% y/y, revenue $108.5m; signs gadolinium offtake with new US aerospace/defence customer
items.summary: MP Materials reported Q2 2026 consolidated revenue and PPA income of $126.1m, comprising $108.5m revenue plus $17.6m PPA income. NdPr production was 840 metric tons (+41% y/y) and NdPr sales 1,006 metric tons (+127% y/y). By segment: Materials generated $95.6m revenue, $17.6m PPA income and $32.5m adjusted EBITDA; Magnetics generated $16.5m revenue and $7.5m adjusted EBITDA. Diluted loss per share was $(0.11); adjusted diluted EPS $(0.01). Strategically, MP signed a long-term offtake agreement with a new American aerospace and defence customer for separated gadolinium, expanding its heavy rare earth (HREE) business, and launched 'Project Swarm' to aggregate demand and standardise specifications for the drone industry, executing subscription agreements with multiple US and allied customers.
items.actionable: For the rare-earth watchlist this is the first hard evidence the volume ramp is real — NdPr sales more than doubled y/y and the Magnetics segment is now adjusted-EBITDA positive. But the company still posted a loss per share, and adjusted EPS came in a cent below consensus. The gadolinium offtake and Project Swarm are the concrete HREE and drone-demand datapoints to track against LYC.AX and UUUU.

items.headline: 5 Aug mixed: Dow gains to a fresh high while S&P and Nasdaq slip from Tuesday's record
items.summary: The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 263.24 points, or 0.5%, to 54,349.12, finishing above Tuesday's record close of 54,085.88. The S&P 500 slipped 12.97 points, or 0.2%, to 7,723.55, holding just below Tuesday's record. The Nasdaq composite fell 221.55 points, or 0.8%, to 26,363.44 and the Russell 2000 fell 17.79 points, or 0.6%, to 3,019.19. Year-to-date at that close: S&P +12.8%, Dow +13.1%, Nasdaq +13.4%, Russell 2000 +21.6%. Breadth was narrow and rotational — Disney advanced on earnings that beat forecasts, helped by "Toy Story 5", while SpaceX fell after announcing increased spending on artificial intelligence. Brent crude held near $79 a barrel and Treasury yields slipped in the bond market.
items.actionable: The Dow/Nasdaq divergence on 5 Aug is the tell: money rotated out of long-duration tech and into cyclicals/value at a 4.6%+ 10Y. That is the same duration trade that governs his HK/China tech sleeve (0700, 1810, 0981) and favours his SG bank exposure (DBS) over growth. VIX at 15.81 means near-zero fear priced — hedges on the levered silver leg were cheap at this point, ahead of the 6 Aug reversal and Friday's payrolls.
